label.reasoning: The item centers on implicit differentiation, including evaluating a slope and finding a second derivative. It requires basic derivative rules for powers and exponentials, the product rule, the chain rule, and higher-order differentiation.

The item centers on implicit differentiation, including evaluating a first derivative and finding a second derivative. It requires basic derivative rules from Unit 2 and chain rule, implicit differentiation, and higher-order derivatives from Unit 3.

Logarithmic differentiation uses implicit differentiation, the chain rule, and logarithmic derivative rules. Finding and classifying the critical point and determining the minimum require analytical applications of derivatives.

Logarithmic differentiation uses implicit differentiation, the chain rule, and derivatives of logarithmic functions. Finding and classifying the critical point and determining the minimum require analytical applications of derivatives.

The central task connects velocity to distance and displacement through integration. Maximizing velocity requires product and chain rules plus extrema analysis; evaluating distance requires integration techniques. Comparing distance and displacement requires interpreting the sign of velocity.

The item requires selecting integration techniques across three integrals: integration by parts, linear partial fractions, and substitution. The definite integral also has an improper endpoint. All required content belongs to Unit 6.

The central task connects velocity to distance and displacement through integration. Maximizing velocity requires product and chain rules and extrema analysis; evaluating the distance integral requires integration by parts. Velocity’s sign determines whether distance equals displacement.

Classifying critical numbers uses the first derivative test. Increasing intervals depend on the sign of f′, while concavity requires differentiating f′ using product and chain rules and interpreting the sign of f″.

Classifying critical numbers primarily uses the first derivative test. Increasing intervals require sign analysis of f′, and concavity requires calculating and interpreting f″, drawing on derivative rules, higher-order derivatives, and analytical applications of differentiation.

The item emphasizes selecting integration techniques: integration by parts for (a), partial fractions for (b), and substitution with an improper endpoint for (c). All required content belongs to Unit 6.

The item centers on a logistic differential equation. Solving the initial-value problem requires separation of variables and integration, while determining long-term concentration requires limits and interpretation of logistic equilibria.

The main task is finding arc length of a planar curve. It requires the power and chain rules to differentiate, the arc-length formula to construct the integral, and antidifferentiation with definite-integral evaluation to obtain the length.
The item centers on convergence and evaluation of an improper integral, using substitution, antiderivatives, and limits at infinity. It does not involve infinite series.

The problem centers on a logistic differential equation. Solving the initial-value problem requires separation of variables and integration; finding the specified time uses that solution. Determining and explaining the limiting concentration requires limits and logistic equilibrium behavior.

The item centers on convergence and evaluation of an improper integral. It requires substitution and antidifferentiation from Unit 6, together with limits at infinity from Unit 1 to determine convergence and evaluate the integral.

The main task is finding the arc length of a planar curve. It requires power-rule and chain-rule differentiation, setting up and simplifying the arc-length integral, and evaluating a definite integral using antiderivatives.

The item focuses on differentiating parametric equations and finding tangent lines, including testing for vertical tangency. Polynomial derivative rules are needed, and limits are required to analyze the tangent slope at the singular parameter value.

The item focuses on parametric differentiation and tangent lines, including vertical-tangent analysis. Polynomial derivatives require Unit 2, and determining the limiting tangent slope at the singular parameter value requires algebraic limit techniques from Unit 1.

The item primarily concerns area enclosed by a polar curve. It also requires polar differentiation for slope and a polar arc-length integral. Basic trigonometric and product-rule derivatives (Unit 2) and definite integration (Unit 6) support these Unit 9 tasks.

The central task uses the alternating series error bound to select a truncation length and determine the remainder’s sign. Explaining convergence also requires the alternating series test. All required content belongs to Unit 10.

The item combines area enclosed by a polar curve, polar slope, and curve length. Polar area is the primary topic. It also requires trigonometric and product-rule differentiation, definite integration, and polar/parametric curve formulas.

The main focus is the alternating series error bound, including choosing the number of terms and determining the remainder’s sign. Explaining convergence also requires the alternating series test. All required content is in Unit 10.

The item tests radius and interval of convergence, including endpoint analysis. Finding the sum function and evaluating the series also require geometric-series identities and power-series manipulation, all within Unit 10.

The central task is determining a power series’ radius and interval of convergence, including endpoint testing. Finding its sum function uses differentiation of a geometric series, and evaluating the series at a specified input uses that sum function.

The central task removes a discontinuity by choosing a value that makes the function continuous. The question also requires algebraic limit evaluation, the derivative definition, and the Intermediate Value Theorem.

The item centers on constructing a Maclaurin expansion, using its terms for approximation, and bounding the truncation error. Derivative rules and higher-order differentiation support constructing the terms; Unit 10 supplies Maclaurin series, polynomial approximations, and error bounds.

The central task removes a discontinuity by choosing a function value consistent with its limit. The item also requires algebraic limit evaluation, the derivative definition, and the Intermediate Value Theorem, drawing on Units 1 and 2.

The item uses a Maclaurin polynomial to approximate a logarithmic value and bound the approximation error. It combines Maclaurin series representation, Taylor polynomial approximation, and an alternating series error bound, all within Unit 10.

The central task is removing a discontinuity by defining the function using its limit. Existence uses the Intermediate Value Theorem, and the limit can be evaluated through the derivative definition, with exponential differentiation and the chain rule.

The item analyzes an implicit curve using first and second derivatives, a tangent line, and local concavity. It requires basic differentiation rules, implicit and higher-order differentiation, and interpreting the second derivative to determine concavity.

The item emphasizes calculating first and second derivatives, including the product rule and exponential derivatives. It also requires constructing a tangent line and using the second derivative to justify concavity at a point.

The central task is removing a discontinuity by defining a function value to match its limit. Other parts require the Intermediate Value Theorem and numerical root estimation. The limit can be evaluated using the derivative definition, exponential differentiation, and the chain rule.

The central task involves calculating first and second derivatives using product, power, and exponential derivative rules. Derivative values determine the tangent line, while the sign of the second derivative justifies concavity.

The item explores an implicit curve through first and second implicit derivatives, a tangent line, and local concavity. It requires basic differentiation rules, implicit and higher-order differentiation, and interpreting the second derivative to determine concavity.

The problem centers on accumulating net inflow using definite integrals. It also requires interpreting a contextual rate of change and using derivative signs and endpoint comparisons to locate and justify an absolute maximum.

The problem centers on accumulating net inflow to determine liquid amounts. It also requires interpreting a rate of change, evaluating definite integrals, and using critical points and endpoints to identify and justify an absolute maximum.

Product and chain rules yield the second derivative; definite integration recovers function values from the given derivative and initial value.

The central concept is differentiating an accumulation function using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and chain rule. Other parts require basic derivative rules, higher-order derivatives, definite integral evaluation via the FTC, and determining an absolute minimum on a closed interval.

The item combines critical points, monotonicity, critical-point classification, concavity, and absolute extrema via the candidates test. It requires derivative rules, calculating a second derivative, and recovering function values from the given derivative and initial value using integration.

Product and chain rules determine the second derivative, while definite integration recovers function values from the initial condition.

Other parts require polynomial differentiation, higher-order derivatives, evaluation of a definite integral using the FTC, and determination of an absolute minimum on a closed interval.

The question analyzes an accumulation function using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. It also requires numerical definite integration, product and chain rules, critical points, increasing intervals, absolute extrema, and concavity.

The parts require selecting and applying integration by parts, partial fractions, improper integration, and polynomial division or substitution. Evaluating the improper integral also requires a limit at infinity.

The question analyzes an accumulation function using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, numerical integration, critical points, increasing intervals, absolute extrema, and concavity. Differentiating the integrand requires product and chain rules.

Euler’s method is the central numerical technique. The tangent-line equation requires derivative interpretation, while finding the exact particular solution of this nonseparable linear differential equation requires integration techniques, including integration by parts.

The item centers on differentiation of parametric equations, including tangent slopes and second derivatives, and also asks for speed and an acceleration vector. It requires basic derivative rules, composite differentiation for the second parametric derivative, and parametric/vector-valued calculus.

Euler’s method is explicitly assessed and compared with an exact solution. Tangent-line construction requires derivative interpretation, while solving the initial-value differential equation requires antidifferentiation and differential-equation techniques.

The item concerns vector-valued particle motion: velocity, acceleration, speed, displacement, and total distance. It requires trigonometric differentiation, vector magnitudes, and integration of speed to determine distance traveled.

The main focus is differentiating parametric equations and finding a tangent line. Additional parts require second derivatives in parametric form and vector-valued speed and acceleration, using polynomial differentiation and the chain rule.

The item concerns motion defined by a vector-valued position function: velocity, speed, acceleration, displacement, and total distance. It requires trigonometric differentiation and integration of speed, together with vector-valued motion concepts.

The central task is deriving and manipulating power-series representations from a geometric series. Differentiation rules are needed for the closed forms, and series convergence concepts are needed to determine the interval of convergence and justify its endpoints.

The central task is deriving power-series representations by differentiating the geometric series, then evaluating a series and determining its interval of convergence. Differentiation rules from Unit 2 are needed to obtain the closed forms; series operations and convergence analysis require Unit 10.

Centers on polar area and its rate of change, with polar-to-Cartesian conversion and polar slope. Requires trigonometric and product-rule differentiation, the chain rule, definite integrals and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and interpretation of a derivative as a contextual rate.

The question centers on polar area and its rate of accumulation, alongside polar coordinates and tangent slopes. It requires basic derivative rules, the chain rule, definite integration, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

The item broadly assesses convergence and divergence of infinite series using named tests, including comparison, the nth-term test, the alternating series test, and the ratio test. All required content belongs to Unit 10.

The item broadly assesses convergence and divergence of infinite series using multiple named tests: comparison, nth-term divergence, alternating series, and ratio. Limit evaluation is needed for the nth-term and ratio tests.

The central task is applying the Lagrange error bound and finding the minimum polynomial degree guaranteeing a specified accuracy. It also requires Maclaurin polynomial approximation and knowledge of exponential derivatives, including higher-order derivatives.

The central task is applying the Lagrange error bound and finding the minimum polynomial degree guaranteeing a specified accuracy. It also involves constructing and evaluating a Maclaurin polynomial and using derivatives of the exponential function to bound the remainder.

The central task is representing a differential-equation solution as a power series. It requires power-rule differentiation, applying the differential equation and initial condition, matching coefficients, identifying a familiar series, and justifying its radius of convergence.

The item centers on a logistic differential equation, including equilibria and stability. It also requires basic differentiation, the chain rule to obtain a second derivative, and analytical reasoning about concavity and maximizing the growth rate.

The item centers on a logistic differential equation, including equilibria, stability, and maximum growth rate. It also requires basic differentiation and the chain rule to obtain the second derivative, plus concavity and optimization reasoning.
